title: What Does a 1,900-Year-Old Birthday Invitation Say?
parts: Northern England. About nineteen hundred years ago.
A woman is planning her birthday party.
She wants one friend to come.
So she writes an invitation.
And it survives.
What does it say?
And is it really the oldest writing by a woman in Latin?
Let's check, one claim at a time.
Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
It is not paper.
It is a thin leaf of wood, written in ink.
It was found at Vindolanda, a Roman fort in northern Britain.
The fort was there before Hadrian's Wall.
The editors say it was found in nineteen eighty-five.
Soil with almost no air kept the wood from rotting.
Today it sits in the British Museum.
The sender is Claudia Severa.
Her husband is Aelius Brocchus.
She writes to Sulpicia Lepidina.
The letter gives the date the Roman way.
The third day before the Ides of September.
That is September the eleventh.
Roughly: please come. Your arrival will make my day happier.
She sends greetings to Lepidina's husband, Cerialis, the fort's commander.
Her husband sends greetings, and, as the editors read it, a little son.
Now look closely at the handwriting.
Idea one: Claudia wrote every word.
Idea two: a scribe wrote every word.
Most of the letter is in one neat, practiced hand.
But the last lines change hand.
The editors say it is quite certain: Claudia added her own goodbye.
Roughly: I shall expect you, sister. Farewell, sister, my dearest soul.
Our reading: like signing a card today.
Two other letters show the same pattern.
Sister? Were they sisters?
Our reading: they were friends, and the word shows affection.
Now the headline: the oldest writing by a woman in Latin.
Careful.
A different Sulpicia, a poet from Augustus's time, would be older.
But some scholars doubt a woman wrote her poems.
Almost certainly, say the editors, Claudia's lines are the earliest known examples of writing in Latin by a woman.
Writing, in her own hand.
Not necessarily the first Latin composed by a woman.
Did Lepidina go? We do not know.
The tablet does not say, and we know of no reply.
So here is what we can say.
It is a real invitation between two real women.
A scribe wrote most of it.
Claudia herself wrote the ending, say the editors. Almost certainly, the oldest Latin handwriting by a woman we know.
The editors date it between the years ninety-seven and one hundred and five.
Our verdict: documented. The letter is real, and the headline needs care.
We usually meet Romans through emperors, battles and speeches.
Here we meet a woman at the edge of the empire.
Hoping her friend will come to her party.
Next time: another everyday question with a surprising answer.
